To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) trust in a manager or professional is based on both affective and cognitive dimensions, and these two types of trust are distinct; (2) affect-based trust is a more important predictor of trust than cognition-based trust; (3) affect-based and cognition-based trust are reciprocally influenced; (4) the development of affect-based trust is based on the quality of the relationship between the manager or professional and the person who is the object of the manager's or professional's trust;

(1) trust is an important and pervasive phenomenon in organizations, and (2) the affect- and cognition-based foundations of trust are both necessary and sufficient to predict trust's development and functioning in organizations.

trust is an important factor in the development and maintenance of effective relationships between managers and professionals in the workplace and that the development of trust depends on the affective and cognitive components of trust.

the nature and functioning relationships of interpersonal trust in organizations.
the development and maintenance of interpersonal trust among individuals who work together in organizational settings.
interpersonal trust in organizations and with its antecedents, consequences, and dynamics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
interpersonal trust is a multidimensional construct that is based on affect and cognition, and that is a foundation for cooperation in the workplace.
trust in close relationships is based on affect and cognition, and that affect-based and cognition-based trust are both important for cooperation.
the trust of managers and professionals in their colleagues is a function of their colleagues' affect and cognitive trustworthiness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the affect- and cognition-based models are not mutually exclusive.
the affect-based and cognitionbased trust dimensions were found to be distinct and both important for the development of trusting relationships.
trust is a complex, multifaceted phenomenon, which can be understood only through the simultaneous consideration of both affective and cognitive components of trust.
The main takeaway from our work is that
interpersonal trust in organizations is a multidimensional construct that can be conceptualized as having both affect-based (emotional) and cognition-based (rational) components.
trust has both affective and cognitive dimensions.

trust is an important factor in the functioning of relationships among managers and professionals, but the factors that contribute to trust's development are not the ones that are commonly believed to do so.
